This study addresses the estimation of a network peer influence model that integrates network structural parameters, regression coefficients, and nonparametric components. We propose using network instrumental variables (NIVs) to identify and apply econometric analysis to network externalities. Specifically, we examine the asymptotic properties of our proposed NIV estimators, demonstrating their convergence rate and semiparametric efficiency. Furthermore, we apply this framework to analyze peer effects within the ANES (American National Election Studies) dataset.

This paper investigates the validity of the Leibniz theorem when applied to Riemann-Lioucker variable-order fractional integral and differential operators. It begins by formulating the variable-order Leibniz theorem specifically for these integral operators, subsequently deriving the corresponding version for the fractional derivative operators through that initial result. The section concludes with several examples designed to illustrate the derived findings.

Spatially variant signal detection represents a fundamental challenge in array processing, where a diffuse source emits signals that arrays must identify and estimate, despite variations in spatial characteristics across the sensor field. This paper addresses the detection of one-dimensional linear signals using a linear array operating in noise. Assuming noise is white and Gaussian, we derive the mean squared error (MSE) for the Recursive Least Squares (RLS) algorithm. By applying this theoretical framework, we evaluate RLS performance in terms of bit error rate (BER) for direct sequence detection in spatially diverse communication networks. Furthermore, the study explores the efficacy of RLS when paired with various spatial prefiltering techniques.

A critical hurdle in analyzing data from modern astronomical surveys is the scarcity of user-friendly tools for creating interactive, web-accessible scientific visualizations. To address this, we present the second version of the survey tools package, known as RCSEDv2. These tools generate highly performant web applications that visualize tabulated data, including spectral energy distributions (SEDs), images, and other image-based datasets using the D3.js JavaScript library. The v2 release introduces a modern, responsive design, a dedicated viewer for spectral data, and a new "compare mode" that allows users to simultaneously display multiple data sources. The software is released under the MIT license and is freely available at https://rcsedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/.

This study examines the kinematic evolution of the Southern Atlantic rift, focusing on the period between 130 and 20 million years ago (Ma), utilizing a comprehensive dataset of 1,050 individual rift segments. By integrating ¹⁴³Nd/¹⁴⁴Nd isotopic signatures, age constraints, and the orientation of these structures, we have delineated three distinct evolutionary phases: (1) an initial phase from 130–80 Ma characterized by N-S trending segments aligned with the Caledonian stress field; (2) a subsequent phase from 80–20 Ma featuring E-W orientation resulting from the reorganization of plate tectonics and the rotation of South America; and (3) a final, post-rift phase dating from 20 Ma onward, defined by the localization of rifting and seafloor spreading into the western and southern basins of the Atlantic, accompanied by the uplift and erosion of the rift valley. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the geological evolution of the South American and African continental margins occurred asynchronously, with the onset of seafloor spreading in the South Atlantic lagging approximately 15 million years behind its initiation in the South Pacific.

Information maximization (IM) serves as an effective semi-supervised learning strategy that relies on unlabelled data, and it has recently been adapted for self-supervised pre-training to leverage vast quantities of such data. Nevertheless, existing research into IM-based segmentation primarily focuses on natural images, where annotated boundaries are easily accessible. In contrast, acquiring annotated medical images is significantly more labor-intensive and costly, creating a constraint that hinders the broader application of IM techniques in medical segmentation. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a novel boundary-sensitive information maximization (BSIM) method designed to enhance the efficacy of boundary utilization during pre-training. The proposed approach achieves this by first reconstructing image patches using gradient descent, a process that inherently generates implicit semantic and structural cues. Building on this foundation, the method trains two encoders to maximize the mutual information between image patches and their corresponding boundaries. Experimental evaluations confirm that the proposed pre-training strategy significantly boosts segmentation performance across multiple downstream tasks.

We introduce a theory-of-mind (ToM)-based methodology designed to enhance the capability of artificial general systems (AGS) in driving complex, multi-turn dialogues within structured yet dynamic environments. To demonstrate this approach, we applied it to the role of a Dungeon Master in Dungeons and Dragons, utilizing this framework to manage interactive gaming sessions. Our experiments reveal that equipping large language models (LLMs) with our proposed ToM module significantly improves their performance in summarizing events, maintaining factual consistency, and executing tasks with intent. Furthermore, we released an open-source, ToM-enhanced Dungeons and Dragons Dungeon Master toolkit to support broader research into human-AI collaboration. All resources, including code and data, are accessible at https://github.com/ChiragAggarwal17/AI-Dungeon-Master.

Discovering vocabulary usage shifts is essential for various fields, including monitoring public sentiment, observing socio-lingistic progress, and adapting older texts for modern readers. We introduce a new method for identifying lexical semantic drift that operates independently of human input, relying solely on word embedding models. This approach maps word concepts into low-dimensional spaces by examining embedding vectors in contrastive pairs of words. We validate our approach on three distinct datasets: two illustrating semantic shifts in sentiment-laden terms and one tracking changes in function words.

We propose new types of $k_\perp$-dependent particle distribution functions applicable to high-energy collisions, specifically targeting the transverse momenta of quarks, antiquarks, and gluons within unpolarized and transversely polarized hadrons. These functions are defined as double transverse-momentum integrals over the standard parton distribution functions (for long distances) or parton density functions (for short distances). The proposed $k_\perp$-dependent functions function as effective "(quasi)particle distribution" metrics that integrate parton dynamics over relevant kinematic scales. Consequently, they yield distinct, experimentally testable predictions for various $z$-dependent and $z$-independent processes, including semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering (SIDIS), Drell-Yan reactions, and gluon or hadron production in hadron-hadron collisions. Conclusive examples are provided for semi-inclusive neutral pion production and the generation of the $\Lambda$ hyperon spin.

Proteins often form complex knots, and understanding how these occur is a significant challenge in topology and molecular biology. We introduce a geometric selection algorithm that utilizes the free energy of protein folding to identify pathways through which a protein knot could spontaneously form from an unknotted state. Applying this method to several knotted proteins, we discovered that the most probable path for a -5.5 knot involves first creating a -4 knot, whereas the optimal initial knot types for the J- knots are a -3 knot and a -6 knot, respectively. Thermodynamic and kinetic analyses indicate that proteins with -5.5 knots take approximately $10^{11}$ years to form such knots, a timeframe far exceeding the current age of the universe; in contrast, formation times for the two -5.5 knot proteins and the two -5.5 knot proteins are approximately $10^{11}$ years, significantly surpassing the age of the universe. Early Dark Energy (EDE) offers a potential solution to the Hubble Tension by boosting the early expansion rate of the universe, thereby increasing the Hubble constant ($H_0$) without altering its current value. Although recent analyses of Planck and Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) data indicate that Early Dark Energy is disfavored by a $\sim 2\sigma$ confidence level, existing studies often rely on standard Bayesian methods that may obscure the full parameter space. To address this, we analyze the latest Planck and BOSS datasets using profile likelihood techniques, concluding that Early Dark Energy remains incompatible with observations at approximately $95\%$ confidence ($\sim 1.9\sigma$). Furthermore, we examine the impact of the $H_0$ prior on these results, demonstrating that the tension between data and the EDE scenario persists even when a prior favoring a higher $H_0$ is applied.

This study introduces a novel category group within the symplectic mapping class group (SMCG) of $\text{bl}_1(\mathbb{T}^4)$, the first four-dimensional torus blown up. We achieve this by initially identifying new generators for the 1-monodromy group of complex structures on $\text{bl}_1(\mathbb{T}^4)$, a result that might hold significance independently. Leveraging these complex structure-related generators, we successfully construct an additional generator for the specified category group in the symplectic mapping class group of the blow-up torus.

In theories featuring spontaneous symmetry breaking, the number of massless Nambu-Goldstone (NG) bosons is determined by the formula $N_{NG} = \dim(G/H)$, where $G$ represents the broken global symmetry group and $H$ its unbroken subgroup. This study examines this theorem within a relativistic and non-relativistic quantum field framework, with a specific focus on $O(N)$ $\sigma$-models. We demonstrate that in non-relativistic systems, this count can be elevated by a contribution of $N/2$ when the unbroken subgroup $H$ exhibits rotational invariance. Furthermore, we clarify the physical origin of these additional modes, identifying them as "Type-II" NG bosons characterized by non-canonical kinetic terms and atypical dispersion relations. Finally, we establish a connection between these unusual modes and the "massless modes" arising from the Wigner-Weyl mechanism in the Wigner class of theories.

Hypothetical Questions (HQs) have recently been shown to significantly boost a model's performance, yet current HQs are typically generated by prompting LLMs with only a single example per query, resulting in limited diversity and utility. To address this, we propose using Disco, a method that distills diverse, high-quality phrasal HQs from LLMs by incorporating a diverse batch of $N$ ($N \ge 1$) support questions during generation. We introduce a diversity-driven sampling strategy to create an optimal batch for each target question and utilize a distillation approach to ensure the generated hypotheses are both challenging and effectively aligned with the target model. Experiments across three datasets demonstrate that integrating these diverse, phrasal HQs via Disco yields substantial performance improvements for base models, particularly for larger variants.

This paper determines both the chromatic number and the equitable yet location-based sum distinguishing chromatic number for various classes of neighbor-based circular graphs. To achieve this, the author first establishes several essential lemmas.

Remote epitaxy is a soft lithographic technique used to grow high-quality films on substrates like graphene, offering advantages such as reduced interfacial interaction, enhanced thermal management, and flexibility in choosing growth conditions. A key benefit of this approach is the ability to control the degree of crystalline alignment, shifting growth from view-domain (single-crystal) to epitaxial polycrystalline states. This study investigates the epitaxial development of the magnetic Heusler alloy Fe$_2$SiAl on graphene supported by sapphire under remote epitaxial conditions. Results demonstrate that the final crystalline structure depends on the substrate's thermal resistance: poor thermal dissipation favors the pinhole epitaxy mode, whereas efficient cooling promotes remote epitaxy. Specifically, Fe$_2$SiAl exhibits a pinhole epitaxial structure on sapphire when graphene is uncoated, but transitions to a fully crystalline state when a 1 nm Al$_2$O$_3$ layer is added. Furthermore, the oxide coating significantly enhances film quality in the pinhole epitaxy regime.

We examine linear codes over the ring $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$, where $p$ is a prime, with a specific focus on determining the dimension and kernel of the parity check matrix. Initially, we address the general case by analyzing the most prevalent subtypes of such codes, specifically $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes constructed via an additive generator. For each variant, we calculate both the code's dimension and the dimensions associated with its kernel. Subsequently, we investigate [R. Gluesing-Dehne et al., *IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory* **64**(10), 5931–5941 (2018)]'s proposed class of codes defined by a specific $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive Cayley method; here, we derive explicit formulas for the dimension and the dimensions of its kernel components. Finally, we explore [X. Z. et al., *arXiv:2305.00000* (2023)]'s [additive] *Cayley* construction for $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, focusing on determining the dimension and kernel dimensions for these structures as well.

This study presents a numerical analysis of the benefits of using polymer plugs instead of continuous polymer injection. The problem is formulated as an optimal control problem with a free final time, where the control variable is the injection rate profile. A novel regularization term is incorporated into the cost functional to penalize fluctuations in the polymer rate. Direct methods are employed to derive the corresponding Hamiltonian system, which in this context becomes a free boundary problem due to the optimized final time. Numerical simulations illustrate the practical application of the theoretical findings.

Current deep learning approaches for medical image diagnosis typically train on well-annotated datasets containing numerous labels. However, the labor-intensive nature of creating these rich labels often results in limited data availability. In contrast, automatically generated labels via pseudo-labeling are abundant and can be easily accessed. This study explores a method to extract high-quality pseudo-labels from single positive labels, leveraging their inherent reliability. We propose a sequential refinement framework that iteratively enhances the accuracy of these self-supervised models. Experiments conducted on two distinct medical image benchmarks demonstrate that our approach yields a significant improvement over existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This work examines the time-fractional phase-field model governed by a time-fractional Ginzburg–Lieb equation, where time differentiation is expressed via the Caputo fractional derivative. Employing a fractional Radau discontinuous Galerkin approach for temporal discretization and a standard finite element method for spatial approximation, we establish a rigorous framework to demonstrate that the model exhibits the diminishing upper bound of energy behavior characteristic of their integer-order counterparts. We also present a comprehensive convergence analysis for the proposed numerical algorithm. Finally, several computational experiments are provided to validate the theoretical findings and illustrate the model's distinct features.

In the framework of rigorous quantum theory, physical systems are defined by von Neumann algebras, and the link between these algebras and their respective Hilbert spaces is established via irreducible representations. We introduce a 2-categorical construction that characterizes states within a specific sub-2-category of Hilbert space functors. This construction defines states on a system's observables as a pair: an underlying state of the system augmented by a pure state on the associated representing Hilbert space. We demonstrate that this new 2-categorical structure maintains an equivalence with the traditional 1-categorical formulation of system states.

The mysterious source of high-energy gamma-rays in the cores of nearby radio galaxies is addressed by our analysis of the nuclei of 150 non-IR-luminous radio galaxies. We employed the 4.5 TeV gamma-ray catalog from the CTA-4.5 TeV Survey, which utilizes data from the VERITAS and H.E.S.S. observatories. Our findings reveal that approximately 15% of these radio galaxy cores emit gamma-rays above 4.5 TeV, with the majority of this emission concentrated in the 4.5–20 TeV range. The source power of these gamma-rays correlates with the power of their core radio emission, yet the source spectra are generally softer than those of active galactic nuclei. We propose that these sources are radiative disks where the central black hole accretes via a disk that terminates at an inner radius larger than the innermost stable circular orbit. In this model, the central black hole accretes at a sub-Eddington rate, and the radio and gamma-ray outputs arise from the dissipation of magnetic energy within the disk.

Investors need to determine how to distribute their investments across various assets. We introduce a Markov decision process (MDP) approach designed to determine this allocation dynamically. Our model accounts for the stochastic nature of asset returns and the potential for investor capital to shift between risk-averse and risk-loving states. We apply these methods to two scenarios: first, optimizing an investment portfolio to achieve the highest expected return, and second, distributing a lottery ticket to maximize expected winnings.

This study introduces an 8-class heart sound categorization framework designed to handle additive noise, convolutional shifts, limitations in low sampling rates, and variations in additive constants. The proposed system integrates eight convolutional neural networks (CNNs), each specialized for a distinct sound type. To achieve this, we developed two key strategies: first, we trained separate models for convolutional deformation and constant shifts using synthetic data generated by applying these transformations to the original sounds; second, we employed distinct architectures for each of the eight sound classes to ensure robustness. Experiments conducted on the public PhysioNet/CinC 2016 dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a mean F1 score of 0.813, a 3.5% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art results.

The rapid advancement of Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) technology has enabled the continuous collection of patient health data through smart devices. Cloud-centric architectures for processing this data, however, raise significant privacy concerns and incur excessive communication costs. Consequently, there is a pressing need for privacy-preserving solutions that are cost-efficient. While current approaches like Fog- and Cloud-based systems address some of these issues, they often overlook data heterogeneity and fail to ensure consistent high-accuracy performance across diverse patient populations. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces **FedHealth**, a novel *Federated Transfer Knowledge* framework designed for wearable health monitoring. This system facilitates the collaborative training of deep learning models among multiple users to detect specific diseases locally. By incorporating model hyperparameter transfer, FedMiner minimizes communication bandwidth usage, and the use of local data ensures privacy is maintained. Furthermore, the approach is optimized to remain effective despite inherent hardware constraints and heterogeneous data distributions. Extensive testing on real-world datasets confirms that the proposed method delivers superior performance in both accuracy and efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines various methods of portfolio optimization that incorporate higher moments such as skewness and kurtosis. These approaches are categorized into two groups: utility-based strategies derived from higher moment utility functions and direct optimization techniques targeting moment measures. This study investigates the interconnections between these methodologies by analyzing the equivalence of specific skewness and kurtosis optimization strategies to the well-known mean-variance optimization framework. Additionally, the paper explores the connections between skewness and kurtosis utilities and optimization strategies involving pseudo-means and pseudo-variances.

We examine the dark energy density within a string theory compactification on a Calabi-Yau threefold, analyzing its evolution across different phases of the moduli space. Our findings indicate that dark energy density remains constant or diminishes as the system evolves, whereas no generic mechanism exists in our model to account for the observed low magnitude of dark energy. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of addressing the cosmological constant problem through string theory dynamics.

Software Automation (SA) is a new system designed to help users with disabilities by automatically generating and managing their assistive software. SA operates on two main pillars: a configuration system and an automation system. The configuration system manages the necessary settings and settings for SA, while the automation system carries out the processes defined by the SA configuration. The authors tested SA on two real-world scenarios, confirming that it is feasible and effective.

This study examines a switching control problem where the cost functions and dynamics of the available regimes are described by ordinary differential equations (ODRs), while regime transition costs are cadl\`ag. The paper characterizes the cost mapping associated with each regime and establishes that the cost function for any strategy is cadl\`ag, thereby guaranteeing that the cost process of the optimal strategy possesses these regularity properties. Furthermore, it is shown that the optimal cost function satisfies the variational formulation of a partial differential integro-differential equation (PDE). Finally, the research investigates the properties of the associated optimal control policy.

This study examines the production of unbalanced numbers of flavorless leptoquarks (LQs) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), a phenomenon resulting from the intrinsic nature of the process. We establish that this mechanism is universal across all LQ models and analyze its implications for future experimental searches. Specifically, we demonstrate that generating final states with an odd count of LQs through standard pair-generation methods is feasible. We further establish the equivalence between creating LQs via uneven pair production and those formed via single production, noting that this avenue could potentially yield odd counts of three or more LQs. Additionally, we establish that the total cross-section for such events remains finite. Finally, we highlight that this novel production channel offers a promising avenue for probing leptoquark properties, particularly in scenarios where the LQ mass approaches the limits of the LHC's capabilities.

We present a novel, efficient algorithm designed to rapidly identify and extract short subsequences from extensive, multi-dimensional temporal sequences. This methodology addresses a critical need in life sciences, where researchers often seek to pinpoint brief events within lengthy observational data. Our approach is grounded in a specific optimization challenge: maximizing the aggregate weighted support of identified subsequences, with support defined by a newly proposed metric. We evaluate the algorithm's performance and practical utility across two distinct domains: single-cell RNA sequencing and the synchronization analysis of physiological rhythms.

Subthermal excitation, a mechanism proposed to explain molecular gas reservoirs in galaxies, involves the pumping of fine-structure transitions via far-infrared (FIR) photons. While this concept has been explored for decades, its application to the neutral carbon (C{\sc i}) lines remains largely untested. In this study, we utilize a suite of semi-analytical models to examine subthermal excitation of C{\sc i} lines within these galactic environments. Our analysis indicates that the optical depth of the gas phase significantly influences the non-thermal brightness temperature of C{\sc i} lines. Specifically, the non-thermal temperature peaks when the gas is optically thin at the first excited state ($J=1\rightarrow0$), reaching a maximum value of approximately $T_{\rm b}^{\rm max}\approx 1.5\,$K. Furthermore, this peak temperature increases with higher dust opacity ($\tau_{\rm dust}$) and dust-to-gas mass ratios ($f_{\rm d/g}$). We also assessed the utility of the $C\,{\sc i}(J=2\rightarrow1)$ line as a tracer for molecular gas mass, comparing it against the standard $J=1\rightarrow0$ line. Our results demonstrate that the $J=2\rightarrow1$ line is more sensitive to variations in $\tau_{\rm gas}$ and $\tau_{\rm dust}$; however, it offers a

We present an explanation for the $B$ and $K$ anomalies observed in binned data, utilizing a model of composite fermions with vector-like mass terms. This framework simultaneously addresses the anomalous decay rates in $b \to s \ell \ell$ and $s \to d \ell \ell$ transitions, as well as the electron and muon mass differences through a specific mechanism: the electron acquires its mass via the Higgs' vacuum expectation value (VEV), whereas the muon obtains its mass primarily through the composite sector, supplemented by a small component from the Higgs VEV.

We examine sequences of permutations where the only constraint on each element is that it maintains a Hamming distance of at least $d$ from every other element in the same sequence. The core challenge involves determining whether these elements collectively determine the entire sequence uniquely. This paper addresses $k$-tuples composed of two independent random permutations multiplied by $(1/d)$, focusing on proving the existence of long sequences that are unambiguously identifiable by their individual parts.

This study introduces a hierarchical few-shot classification framework designed to identify faulty musical instruments. While previous research has concentrated on large-scale datasets containing thousands of distinct instruments, this work addresses the challenge of recognizing instruments within datasets characterized by both numerous categories and very limited sample counts per category. The proposed method leverages a hierarchy that organizes instruments into broader groups based on shared acoustic traits, thereby facilitating recognition even when only a few examples are available. Experiments conducted on the Musical Instrument Classification (MID) dataset demonstrate that this two-tiered approach yields superior performance compared to standard few-shot classification strategies, particularly in scenarios involving extremely limited training data.

We introduce a dataset comprising 5,800 questions and answers derived from 1,600 research papers. These questions are designed to be answerable exclusively using information found within the supporting literature, often necessitating synthesizing information from multiple sources to form a complete response. Our questions target diverse difficulty levels and rely on various types of supporting evidence. Additionally, we provide a dataset of 10,000 questions and answers from 2,500 papers, which serves as a benchmark for comparative analysis. We present the methodology for generating this dataset, along with evaluations of various question-answering models using both our primary dataset and the comparison dataset. Finally, we assess the utility of our dataset for supporting knowledge acquisition by human participants. Human study results indicate that providing learners with this dataset enhances their ability to locate relevant information in research papers when seeking answers.

We examine the computational efficiency and accuracy of pulsar timing array signals generated by inspiralling eccentric binaries when modeled using both the standard approximation and the exact strong-field expressions for periastron advance, semi-latus rectum, and gravitational wave energy flux. Our findings indicate that standard approximations introduce significant errors in the induced signals at high eccentricities, with these discrepancies growing as the signal-to-noise ratio increases. We analyze the specific impact of omitting precise calculations for the three key parameters governing the strong-field effects. Furthermore, we assess the processing times for simulations involving various numerical integration techniques, comparing them against the efficiency of the proposed method.

Starting from a configuration where particles occupy all positive integers, the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) on the integers features a dynamic element such that, when scaled down, the system's evolution converges to the ASEP aggregation time. The scaling limit of the ASEP aggregation time can be characterized as the trajectory of a stochastic process known as the ASEP velocity process. This process operates under a scaling framework where $N$ particles are involved, and it is defined by a parameter $\theta N$. The scaling limit of the ASEP velocity process is described in detail, and it is demonstrated that this process adheres to a functional central limit theorem.

This study examines the utility of mathematical modeling in representing biological systems, with a specific focus on infectious disease outbreaks. It explores the theoretical underpinnings, classifications, and validation of such models. The authors highlight the advantages of mathematical modeling in offering a rigorous, unambiguous language for describing system dynamics, facilitating their simulation, and enabling hypothesis testing through empirical data analysis. Specifically within the context of the current pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2, the paper investigates the historical development of epidemic models and analyzes how various models were employed to characterize the virus's transmission, estimate key epidemiological parameters, forecast future trends, and assess potential intervention strategies.

A Majorana fermion represents a unique fermion that serves as its own antiparticle, governed by the Majorana equation and subject to Majorana conditions. This study examines the probability density distribution of Majorana fermions across various scenarios, including those where they are confined to one dimension, exhibit free movement, follow Fermi-Dirac statistics, are subject to an external potential, encounter obstacles, interact with other particles, or exist within chaotic systems. Additionally, it investigates the entropy associated with entangled Majorana fermions. The findings indicate that probability density for these self-conjugate particles mirrors that of standard Dirac or complex Majorana fermions when specific constraints apply, such as in cases of confinement, freedom, or Hermitian coupling. Conversely, for non-Hermitic interactions, the density distribution of linear Majorana fermions diverges from that of complex fermions.

Acronyms are a ubiquitous feature of technical English, serving as space-saving abbreviations for frequently used phrases. Despite their prevalence, these terms often create comprehension barriers for non-native English speakers who lack specific vocabulary knowledge. Furthermore, even fluent readers may struggle when encountering an acronym whose expanded form is unknown, as the meaning cannot always be inferred from context alone. To address these challenges, we introduce **MadDog**, a web-based platform designed to help users look up acronyms and their corresponding definitions. MadDog supports multiple languages for both the search query and the definition results. Additionally, it offers mechanisms to report new acronyms and submit corrections to existing entries, ensuring the resource remains accurate and comprehensive.

Gross et al. introduced the concept of the BCS-BEC crossover in ultracold fermionic gases over a decade ago, an achievement that earned them the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics. Central to this phenomenon is the transformation of atom pairs into tightly bound molecular states, a process known as the spinor atom-molecule transition. This occurs when a Feshbach resonance facilitates the conversion of a second, repulsive molecular state into a weakly bound dimer. While experimental progress has been substantial, theoretical models have predominantly focused on weakly interacting systems. This study investigates the regime of strong interactions, demonstrating that the conversion of a repulsive to a weakly bound molecular state can be achieved directly through three-body recombination involving two atoms and one molecule. Our findings indicate that this method enables the creation of spinor molecules with negative binding energies, offering a distinct advantage over standard two-body resonance techniques, which are constrained to negative spin configurations.

We introduce DNAFile, a novel framework for organizing hierarchical information encoded in DNA. DNAFile supports the creation of DNA molecules (referred to as pages) via automatic primer design and synthesizes these pages using an external DNA storage system. By enabling data updates and deletion, our framework contrasts with current DNA storage methods, which typically suffer from inefficient data retrieval and lack support for modifications. DNAFile employs a B-tree structure to facilitate efficient data queries. Furthermore, our proposed G-repair algorithm ensures data consistency by maintaining the integrity of DNA pages following updates. Experimental results demonstrate that DNAFile reduces query times by 1.5 times and decreases the quantity of required DNA DNA by 1.5 times relative to existing DNA storage systems.

Topological insulators and superconductors are characterized by global topological invariants, which can be decomposed into local contributions originating from singularities in momentum space, such as Dirac points, Weyl points, and nodal lines. This review examines the local topological indicators applicable to various three-dimensional topological singularities. It further surveys recent developments in observing these indicators experimentally, specifically within photonic systems, as well as in electronic, phononic, and circuit electrical platforms.

Brain tumors represent a prevalent and perilous neurological disorder, necessitating the development of robust diagnostic systems to support clinicians. Deep learning-driven approaches have demonstrated significant potential in this domain, yet current deep learning models often demand extensive datasets and generate "black box" predictions lacking interpretability. Addressing these limitations, we introduce a "two-in-one" framework grounded in a multi-task learning architecture with attention mechanisms for the detection and classification of brain tumors. This framework utilizes an attention-directed U-Net framework for segmentation and a DenseNet framework for classification tasks. The incorporation of attention mechanisms enables the model to concentrate on critical anatomical regions, while multi-task learning leverages task correlation to enhance overall performance through shared feature representations. Furthermore, the integration of dense connections within the classification module facilitates the effective reuse of extracted features. Extensive experiments conducted on the prominent "Brain Tumor Segmentation" (BraTS) 2019 dataset confirm that this framework achieves a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.8989 for segmentation and an accuracy of 0.9691 for classification, substantiating its high efficacy.

Optimizing differentiable rendering systems and inverse problem solvers often conflicts, as artists require computationally cheap shadow calculations for manual parameter tuning, whereas inverse problem algorithms demand high precision to ensure convergence. This paper introduces a new approach that delivers high-precision, efficient, and fully differentiable shadow calculations. The method introduces a specific differentiable rendering equation, which incorporates a closed-form solution for soft shadows cast by area lights. Tests indicate that this technique offers a substantial performance boost over standard Monte Carlo methods while maintaining robust gradient flow for optimization tasks.

Motion deinterlacing serves as a crucial image enhancement technique for systems handling interlaced video inputs, addressing issues like missing data and visual artifacts caused by the inherent limitations of the interlacing method. This study introduces a new approach, termed MDI (Motion-Driven Interpolation), which leverages motion estimation to recover the full progressive frames from interlaced frames. Once reconstructed, convolutional neural networks (CNNs utilize motion information to interpolate the opposite field and eliminate motion artifacts. Specifically, this model employs two distinct branches: one calculates horizontal pixel values and the other handles vertical pixel values for the target full frame. A key innovation is the use of a unified architecture capable of handling various motion directions without needing extra motion compensation steps. This streamlined design allows for extremely efficient processing, enabling real-time performance on a single GPU while delivering superior interpolation accuracy compared to existing methods.

An extensive analysis of neutron skin thickness in neutron stars, as well as the related rms radii of free neutron gases, is conducted within the context of nuclear physics. This study examines the connection between nuclear matter properties, the properties of the equation of state, and the behaviors observed in neutron stars. A comparative assessment of the non-relativistic and relativistic frameworks of nuclear mean-field theory is performed, with a specific focus on the APR3 equation of state. Additionally, the implications for the determination of the rms radius characterizing the surface distribution of protons versus neutrons in ${}^{208}\text{Pb}$ are discussed.

Accurately forecasting flood events is a critical priority for emergency response agencies tasked with safeguarding lives and property. This forecasting relies heavily on numerical simulations of the two-dimensional shallow water equations (2D SWE), a process that demands considerable computational resources. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to quickly solve the 2D SWE, utilizing a multi-scale residual neural network architecture augmented with a lightweight short-term memory module. This integration enables the model to effectively capture the multi-scale characteristics of flow fields while maintaining high computational efficiency. Trained on a comprehensive dataset of over 1.5 million boundary value problems covering diverse geometries and flow conditions, the network demonstrates remarkable accuracy in predicting flow variables, including free surface elevation, velocity, and direction. When used to predict flood inundation, the solver matches the precision of traditional methods but executes solutions approximately 100 times faster. Furthermore, it generalizes effectively to unseen geometries and flow scenarios, offering a robust framework for the rapid resolution of the 2D SWE.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging a set of exposures taken at varying levels, a process that naturally improves contrast and color saturation. Although HDR has long been standard for digital cameras, the limited screen real estate of smartphones often makes it difficult for users to notice these visual enhancements. Furthermore, capturing the required bracketed exposures demands user initiative, which can be inconvenient. This study introduces an HDR system designed to operate automatically on smartphones, streamlining the user experience. The proposed solution utilizes a deep-learning-driven exposure selection algorithm to determine the optimal bracketing scheme in real time, ensuring that exposure transitions remain imperceptible to the user. Additionally, the system employs a fusion technique based on weighted averaging, where exposure levels are integrated into the weighting scheme. Evaluations using both synthetic and real-world scenes confirm that this automatic HDR framework matches the quality of manually controlled HDR methods.

Deep learning has become a cornerstone of modern science, yet it often functions as a "black box," obscuring the internal mechanisms that yield specific outcomes. To address this opacity, researchers have developed various interpretability tools; however, a critical hurdle remains: the vast array of available methods makes it difficult for scientists to navigate and select the most appropriate technique for their specific research questions. We propose a structured framework designed to clarify these choices by categorizing deep learning interpretability methods according to the distinct needs of different research domains. Furthermore, we offer practical guidance on selecting and applying these methods effectively. Finally, we illustrate our framework's utility by applying interpretability tools to the analysis of galaxy morphology.

A fundamental understanding of temperature distribution is essential for optimizing the performance of industrial processes, particularly those involving highly exothermic reactions. This study employs real-time, rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine temperature arrangements within a catalytic fixed bed during an exothermic reaction. The process utilizes a bed of γ-alumina pellets, with reaction heat generated by the dehydrogenation of cyclohexane. The findings reveal a temperature gradient forming vertically through the bed due to restricted heat dissipation along the axial direction. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the temperature distribution becomes increasingly non-uniform as cyclohexane conversion rates rise.
This note explores the connection between stable mapping theory and 3-manifold topology, offering a unified proof of both the M. Mirro conjecture and its associated consequences.

Simulating patient-specific cardiac mechanics simulations is essential for understanding disease progression and evaluating treatments. These simulations are typically modeled using nonlinear elasticity, which demands computationally intensive solvers capable of handling complex, anatomically accurate geometries. This study compares several multilevel preconditioners for these solvers, including algebraic multigrid (AMG), geometric multigrid (GMG), and full multigrid with geometric coarsening (FMG), to evaluate their computational efficiency. The results demonstrate that both AMG and FMG offer superior efficiency relative to standard Gauss-Seidel methods and other multilevel approaches. Furthermore, the findings indicate that combining AMG with geometric coarsening yields optimal performance.

The non-crossing partition approach, introduced by Borodin, Prendivale, and Corwin, provides an analytical method for determining joint eigenvalue densities of specific ensembles of random symmetric or Hermitian matrices where row elements follow independent distributions. This work broadens that framework by incorporating non-zero correlation between the upper triangular components of these matrices, utilizing a generalized family of orthogonal polynomials defined on weighted non-negative Bessel processes. These extensions encompass two notable cases: the ensemble of matrices with truncated exponential distribution on their upper triangle (encompassing zero correlation) and the ensemble with geometric distribution on their upper triangle (encompassing all nonzero correlations).

Persuasive technology empowers users to influence others' attitudes and behaviors, with video formats being particularly effective for this purpose. Although persuasive AI-generated videos have become a rapidly expanding field, they lack a comprehensive review. This paper introduces a unified persuasive taxonomy and examines state-of-the-art techniques along with promising future directions. Specifically, we analyze generation strategies for three primary video types: those aiming to instill confidence in virtual characters, those designed to promote specific products, and those intended to advocate certain viewpoints. We further address emerging methodologies leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Finally, we outline significant challenges and propose potential avenues for subsequent investigation.

Security measures are often adopted because they appear necessary, yet the extent to which these solutions mask underlying vulnerabilities is unclear. This study investigates the impact of visual security indicators on hacking behavior through a controlled experiment involving 100 participants who accessed 100 distinct target systems. Results reveal that the presence of security stickers or logos significantly increases hacking attempts, with attack rates nearly doubling compared to targets lacking such markers. Furthermore, the presence of these visual cues had no influence on the severity of attacks, suggesting that while their visibility deters hacking behavior, it does not necessarily prevent determined individuals from exploiting security flaws.

The diffraction of light and sound can be controlled by engineering acoustic surface structures that interact with light at the nanoscale. While this capability enables advanced optical devices, it necessitates manufacturing techniques capable of producing high-precision relief patterns at micro- and nanometer scales. Furthermore, for applications involving acoustic light-matter interactions, there is a specific need to generate features smaller than the acoustic wavelength, which is typically in the micrometer range. We demonstrate the fabrication of microacoustic metagratings with a periodicity of 1.5 µm at ultra-high frequencies of 100 MHz using direct laser writing via two-photon polymerization. Acoustic microscopy and atomic force microscopy confirm the accuracy of these surfaces. Acoustical measurements reveal that our devices generate distinct first- and second-order diffraction orders at 100 MHz, validating their functionality. Finally, we propose that microacoustic metagratings fabricated through this method serve as a versatile platform for developing acoustic devices operating at high frequencies.

This study examines diffusion processes where the spatial variability of the diffusivity follows random patterns. We analyze the long-term behavior of the probability density function (PDF) for particle positions, specifically focusing on cases where the spatial diffusivity converges asymptotically to a stable distribution with index $\beta$ (where $0 < \beta < 2$). Our analysis indicates that, asymptotically, particle displacement follows super-diffusion characterized by a scaling exponent of $\frac{2}{\beta}$, while its shape evolves toward a non-Gaussian form with a fixed, process-dependent tail. To substantiate these findings, we examine two concrete examples: standard Brownian motion constrained by an infinite square well and a specific class of time-fractional fractional diffusion equations (fractional Fokker-Planck equations).

This paper presents a novel theory grounded in the concept of general coupled modes to explore interactions between optical resonators, waveguide modes, and both linear as well as Kerr nonlinear optical effects. By applying this framework to derive the Generalized Coupled Mode Equations (GCME), the study elucidates how the coupling coefficients for linear energy exchange are determined by the overlap integrals of interacting mode fields and their respective coupling coefficients for Kerr nonlinear cross-phase modulation (XPM) are similarly linked to mode overlap characteristics. A primary advantage of this approach lies in its capacity to account for mutual influences among multiple resonators and waveguide modes, thereby facilitating a comprehensive analysis of linear coupling dynamics and nonlinear optical behaviors within these integrated systems. To demonstrate the model's efficacy, specific illustrations are provided concerning linear resonator coupling and the generation of soliton molecules via nonlinear resonator interactions.

This study extends established results on global asymptotic stability (GAS) for systems with unbounded controls by presenting a Lyapunov theorem tailored to exponentially stable (ES) systems with unbounded controls. It further derives several corollaries that serve as useful tools in designing control systems. This study introduces a super-resolution (SR) reconstruction method utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework to recover high-resolution velocity fields from low-resolution data for Rayleigh-Bénard convection across various Reynolds numbers. The proposed SR-GAN model was trained on turbulent flow data (Re = 2.86 × 10⁴) and demonstrated the capability to accurately reconstruct velocity fields at unreached conditions (Re = 10³ and Re = 4 × 10⁴) with training data restricted to lower thresholds. Comparative analysis using standard bicubic interpolation revealed that the SR-GAN approach significantly outperforms it in capturing flow structures, particularly small-scale features. Furthermore, the method effectively recovers large-scale structures and flow dynamics even when generating resolutions up to 20 times higher than the input. These findings indicate that SR-GAN serves as a robust tool for enhancing experimental resolution and provides a powerful means for extracting flow characteristics from data obtained at Reynolds numbers outside the trained range.

Uncertainty modeling stands as a critical challenge in open-world image recognition, particularly given the continuous influx of unseen classes. Current approaches often rely on extensive supervised datasets and are constrained to closed environments, failing to address these specific limitations. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel framework that shifts from supervised to self-supervised learning, enabling deployment across any scene containing both known and unknown categories. Our method models uncertainty as a function of driven energy, which quantifies the difficulty a model faces in distinguishing a sample from classifiable images. Leveraging this insight, we propose a new calibration technique that uses energy to estimate uncertainty, subsequently updating the model's output probabilities. Extensive tests confirm that this approach requires no additional labeled data for known or unknown classes, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and robustness.

Although significant progress has been made in applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) across various domains, the field still lacks standardized metrics and tools to properly assess the performance of RL algorithms using Lifelong Learning (LL) frameworks. This study introduces Lif2Explorer, a new evaluation environment designed to test RL methods within an LL setting. The system provides a suite of interconnected levels, each with its own distinct reward mechanism, alongside a platform for evaluating RL approaches in both finite and continuous (open-ended) LL scenarios. Additionally, we propose a new set of metrics specifically for assessing RL in open-ended LL contexts and demonstrate the framework's utility by evaluating three prominent RL methods.

Process mining has grown significantly over the last ten years, offering methods to extract valuable insights from event logs. This paper introduces a novel approach to process exploration that utilizes streaming technology. The proposed method involves continuously monitoring running processes to automatically generate an implicit process model by identifying behavior patterns, a technique that bypasses the need for manual model construction. The core of this approach is an innovative, flexible model representation that captures both structural elements and behavioral aspects of processes. The authors evaluate the proposed technique through a practical case study, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Liger, a new high-throughput near-infrared (NIR) spectrograph recently installed at the W.M. Keck Observatory, is designed to achieve a spectral resolution of 1000 with a spectral efficiency of 40%. To meet these performance metrics, the system incorporates a novel data processing architecture featuring a dual-stage filtering approach and a high-speed 10 Gbps Fibre Channel interface. This paper details the design and implementation of the software framework supporting Liger's hardware architecture, addressing the integration of drivers, the implementation of the data stream, and the creation of the software interface for the instrument.

Multiplexing spatial modes of single-photon wavepackets enables the creation of high-efficiency, multi-dimensional quantum key distribution channels. This study introduces a novel technique for spatial mode analysis using entangled photon pairs, offering a twofold enhancement in efficiency and a reduction in analysis times compared to standard single-photon methods. The approach leverages the enhanced precision of state analysis via quantum correlations to employ a pair of remotely prepared, entangled photons in spatial mode reconstruction. Numerical simulations confirm this strategy is effective for distinguishing overlapping Laguerre-Gauss modes, exhibiting improved discrimination fidelity and resolving smaller topological charge differences than previously achievable.

Let $S$ be a smooth moduli space of stable compactly supported codimension $c$ subvarieties within a smooth variety $X$ of dimension $n$, where $n \geq 2$ and $c \geq 1$. We construct an algebraic smooth thickening of $S$ into a space $U$, which parametrizes first-order algebraic extensions. Furthermore, we identify this space $U$ with a smooth smooth submanifold inside the space of subschemes that possess an specified extension of their normal sheaf over an open dense subset. For the specific case where subvarieties are curves, we determine the total class of the bundle of first extensions over $U$ in terms of the topological characteristics of $S$.

Eco-epidemiological systems are characterized by diverse dynamic behaviors, including transients that can endure for extended periods. These persistent states offer valuable indicators for forecasting abrupt shifts in population structures and can inform the creation of early warning mechanisms for their detection. This study focuses on a specific two-timescale model within eco-epidemiology, which incorporates a carrying capacity and a timescale ratio parameter ($\epsilon$) approaching zero. By conducting a singularity analysis, the research identifies a Hopf bifurcation boundary separating stable coexistence from limit cycle oscillations. Intriguingly, the analysis reveals that the locus of transcritical bifurcation, where the system transitions from host extinction to coexistence, intersects the locus of the persistent Hopf oscillations. This intersection creates a distinct region of coexistence characterized by high host and host populations. Notably, the authors observe that the coexistence via long-term transients exists independently of the standard immediate coexistence zone. The primary contribution of this research is the identification of a unique mechanism for early warning detection: the divergence of the coexistence path along the transient timescale, which converges toward the stable coexistence point. This phenomenon occurs regardless of the initial population configuration and is triggered by moderate increases in the carrying capacity.

Observations indicate a turnover in the galaxy stellar mass–specific star formation rate (GSFMR) relation at high masses, where the slope becomes negative. While the underlying cause remains unclear, we propose that central supermassive black holes are responsible for this downturn. By running semi-analytic models across a broad range of parameters, we demonstrate that active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback is necessary to produce the observed negative slope in the mass–specific star formation relation. Furthermore, we show that feedback efficiency must decline as galaxy mass increases to accurately match data. This decline allows for robust star formation quenching in massive galaxies while preserving star formation activity at lower mass ranges.

Cross-lingual sentiment analysis (CLSA) facilitates mining public opinion on diverse languages, yet developing CLSA models for low-resource languages remains challenging due to data scarcity. This study introduces a new CLSA framework for Indonesian and English that leverages additional training data from English to enhance Indonesian performance despite limited Indonesian availability. Furthermore, the framework supports multi-source training using different ID-EU sentiment datasets, allowing the model to benefit from these variations. Experiments confirm that proposed models achieve state-of-the-art results for Indonesian sentiment classification and demonstrate effective cross-lingual capability.

Fences serve as a synchronization mechanism in concurrent programming, ensuring that memory updates made before a fence are visible to other threads only after the fence itself executes. This work introduces two novel operations for 64‑bit x86 fences: self‑invalidation and self‑degradation. A self‑invalidating fence guarantees visibility of preceding updates solely if those updates actually occur (a property akin to strong ordering). Conversely, a self‑degrading fence permits updates to become visible even if the fence executes before they are issued (reminiscent of release‑acquire semantics). We demonstrate that these new operations can be efficiently realized on x86 architecture. Furthermore, we illustrate their utility by employing self‑invalidating and self‑degrading fences to resolve several concurrent programming challenges within Java.

The classical Freiman $3k-4$ theorem states that for a prime $p \ge 3$, any subset $A \subset \mathbb{Z}_p$ with cardinality $|A| \ge \frac{3}{4}k$ possesses a small covering set $C$ such that $|C|$ is bounded linearly by $k$ (specifically, $|C| \le \frac{3}{4}k$) and $A \subset C$. The authors introduce a robustified version of this result, demonstrating that for prime $p \ge 3$, if $A \subset \mathbb{Z}_p$ has size $|A| \ge \frac{3}{4}k$, then there exists a subset $B \subset A$ with $|B| \le C\cdot\frac{3}{4}k$ (where $C$ is an absolute constant) such that every element in $A$ can be expressed as the sum of two elements from $B$ (i.e., $A \subset B+B$).

Let $B$ denote a fractional Brownian motion in $\mathbb{R}$ with parameter $H \in (0,1)$, considered with fixed non-zero drift. By applying the method of characteristics to the associated parabolic partial differential equation, we demonstrate that for any $t > 0$, the push-forward of Lebesgue measure by the path $B_t$ assigns positive mass to specific Borel sets possessing non-empty interiors; furthermore, the distribution of $B_t$ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure for such $t$. Additionally, for any $T > 0$, the trajectory $\{B_s : s \in [0,T]\}$ possesses Hausdorff dimension $D_H^f = \min\{1, H\}$. Consequently, for any Borel subset $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ with $D_H^f(A) < 1$, both the image set $\{B_s + \mu s : s \in A\}$ and the measure of $\{B_s + \mu s : s \in A\}$ are zero for any fixed non-zero constant $\mu$. As a result, for any fixed non-zero $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and the same drift condition, if $A$ is a Borel subset of $[0,T]$ with the specified dimension constraint, then both the image set under the drifted process and its associated measure vanish

Dirac's variational method, enhanced by the Jackiw-Kerman functional, is employed to investigate the quantum behavior of the H\'enon-Heiles model within a disorder environment. This study examines two distinct types of quantum randomness: discrete two-level fluctuations and continuous Gaussian randomness. By analyzing the ground state properties and excited state dynamics, the study addresses the breakdown of the correspondence principle and the phenomenon of quantum localization. Results indicate that the model's inherent chaotic potential and the nature of the introduced external disorder cooperatively determine the degree of quantum suppression of classical chaos and the extent of localization in the system.

This study introduces a novel approach to predict ICU admissions for COVID-19 patients by analyzing standard chest X-rays. This method addresses a critical need, as isolating infected individuals to prevent viral spread is vital, yet obtaining CT scans for every individual is often unfeasible. While CT scans are highly effective for diagnosing COVID--19, their requirement for extensive medical resources limits widespread screening. Consequently, this paper explores whether ICU admission status can be predicted using only chest X-rays. The authors developed a model that classifies images into two categories: those likely to result in ICU admission and those not. The model was trained on a dataset of 1,500 labeled images and achieved an 88% accuracy rate. This approach offers a valuable tool for healthcare providers to identify patients requiring intensive monitoring, thereby optimizing resource allocation.

We demonstrate that the universally simplicial group $ \mathbb{D}_U $, with respect to Eda's duality for simplicial sets, exists. This finding implies the presence of a monoidal structure on the category of simplicial groups, further leading to the confirmation that $ \mathbb{D}_U $ itself functions as the universally simplicial group within the category of all universal simplicial groups. Consequently, a universally dual duality is established for the category of simplicial sets. This result is achieved by defining a specific simplicial group $ \mathbb{D}_U $ through the application of Eda's dualization process on Kan's universally weak group structures found in the category of all sets. Additionally, it is proven that $ \mathbb{D}_U $ embodies the universal simplicial group relative to the framework of Eda duality. As a secondary outcome, this research confirms the validity of a broader dualization procedure proposed by the author, which extends the logic behind the dualization of abelian groups and chain complexes into the domain of higher algebraic structures.

Visual relationship detection (VRD) serves as a pivotal yet challenging task within the domain of visual language understanding. Although current models have achieved promising outcomes, they frequently generate numerous incorrect predictions stemming from three primary issues: (1) hallucinated objects, (2) spurious prepositional phrases, and (3) pre-trained biases. This paper offers a comprehensive analysis of each of these specific errors. We introduce a systematic framework designed to identify and mitigate them by integrating a diverse array of strategies. Experimental outcomes indicate that this approach yields a significant boost in both micro- and macro-F1 scores across two prominent benchmarks, specifically COCO and Visual Genome.

We introduce Delta Sampling R-Action (R-Action) for video action recognition under challenging conditions, such as limited data or poor lighting. This method builds upon the state-of-the-art Restricted Frame Interpolation (FRI) video encoding, which has been recently introduced. Specifically, we propose a delta sampling strategy for video encoding that is tailored to specific issues like data scarcity and adverse lighting. When paired with fine-tuning, this strategy enables R-Action to effectively handle those difficulties. Experiments indicate that the delta sampling R-Action outperforms other models on both public benchmarks and our newly created datasets featuring low-light scenarios.

We introduce a novel FPGA architecture designed to execute database operations, specifically content-addressable concurrent processing (CAC). This approach enables database queries to be executed directly in hardware, eliminating the need to transfer data between storage and memory architectures. While previous attempts at database architecture implementation on FPGAs have been constrained by limited data movement bandwidth, this new design addresses that issue through the use of a hierarchical memory system. This system organizes data into multiple levels based on depth, utilizing a sorting algorithm to facilitate rapid navigation. Additionally, we implemented the CAC design using an Altera Nios II soft CPU and evaluated its performance through various database content-accessible queries.

We present 100 snapshots from a high-resolution hydrodynamic simulation of a massive galaxy group at a redshift of approximately 3, utilizing an initial mass of $1.0 \times 10^{12} \, M_{\odot}$. Initially, the dominant member exhibits a gas-rich, grand-design stellar-disk with significant asymmetry. Over the course of 4.5 billion years, the system evolves into a quiescent $E$-type elliptical galaxy, characterized by a large-scale stellar halo and a central bulge with a bulge-to-total mass ratio of roughly 0.4. The formation of this central bulge is driven by an intense, galaxy-wide starburst event peaking around 2.5 billion years into the simulation. This starburst results from the gravitational collapse of a central, massive, rotationally supported gas disk, a process facilitated by the accretion of a satellite galaxy and the internal evolution of the host system. Notably, the primary galaxy retains its main body throughout, distinguishing this scenario from those involving major mergers. While the satellite's interaction triggers the initial collapse, the starburst reaches its maximum intensity only after the satellite has been fully disrupted and its material dispersed. Consequently, the simulation demonstrates that the formation of central bulges can occur through the long-term dynamical evolution of minor satellite interactions within stable systems, rather than exclusively through violent merger events.

The authors propose a novel methodology for conducting a comprehensive Bayesian re-analysis of the "Universal Texture Zero" of Flavor (UZZF) framework. This study aims to rigorously examine the model's capacity to account for neutrino oscillation data, recent measurements from the Belle II experiment regarding lepton flavor violation, and recent findings on rare meson decays, specifically $B \to K \ell^+ \ell^-$ and $K \to \pi \ell^+ \ell^-$. By rigorously integrating recent experimental results, the research updates the analysis of the model's parameters, specifically the three complex entries located off the diagonal within the neutrino mass matrix. The study employs a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to rigorously explore the posterior probability distribution of these parameters, given the observed data. The results indicate that the UZZF model remains consistent with current experimental constraints, successfully accommodating neutrino oscillation data and recent results from Belle II, while simultaneously predicting a branching fraction for the $\mu \to e \gamma$ decay that aligns with recent observations from the MEG II experiment. Furthermore, the study projects potential sensitivities for upcoming experiments, specifically the Mu3e collaboration, regarding the $\mu \to e \text{e}^-$ decay channel.

Current approaches to neural program generation typically involve training models to predict the next line of code, a method that offers limited capacity for learning complex control flow structures. To address this, we propose a new framework for neural-driven program synthesis that incorporates static program analysis. In our approach, a neural component learns to suggest code fragments which, when combined with automatically inferred fragments via flow-sensitive data flow analysis, result in a program satisfying specified inputs and outputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by applying it to a data-centric sorting algorithm, highlighting how neural models trained under these constraints can master intricate input-output mappings and generate efficient sorting code.
